[[File:Sine oscillations.jpg|thumb|right|300px|[[Sine and cosine|Sine]] oscillations {{math|1=''F'' = 0.01}}]]

In the study of [[dynamical system]]s, the '''Biryukov equation''' (or '''Biryukov oscillator'''), named after Vadim Biryukov (1946), is a [[Nonlinear system|non-linear]] second-order [[differential equation]] used to model damped [[oscillation|oscillators]].<ref>H. P. Gavin, The Levenberg-Marquardt method for nonlinear least squares curve-fitting problems (MATLAB implementation included)</ref>

The equation is given by 
<math display=block>\frac{d^2 y}{dt^2}+f(y)\frac{dy}{dt}+y=0, \qquad\qquad (1) </math>

where {{math|''ƒ''(''y'')}} is a piecewise [[constant function]] which is positive, except for small {{mvar|y}} as

<math display=block>\begin{align}
& f(y) = \begin{cases} -F, & |y|\le Y_0; \\[4pt] F, & |y|>Y_0. \end{cases} \\[6pt]
& F = \text{const.} > 0, \quad Y_0 = \text{const.} > 0. 
\end{align}</math>

Eq. (1) is a special case of the [[Lienard equation]]; it describes the auto-oscillations.

Solution (1) at separate time intervals when f(y) is constant is given by<ref>Arrowsmith D. K., Place C. M. Dynamical Systems. Differential equations, maps and chaotic behavior. Chapman & Hall, (1992)</ref>

<math display=block> y_k(t) = A_{1,k}\exp(s_{1,k}t) + A_{2,k}\exp(s_{2,k}t) \qquad\qquad (2)</math>

where {{math|exp}} denotes the [[exponential function]]. Here 
<math display=block>s_k = \begin{cases} 
\displaystyle \frac{F}{2}\mp\sqrt{ \left(\frac{F}{2}\right)^2-1}, & |y|<Y_0; \\[2pt]
\displaystyle -\frac{F}{2}\mp\sqrt{ \left(\frac{F}{2}\right)^2-1} & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}</math>
Expression (2) can be used for real and complex values of {{mvar|s{{sub|k}}}}.

The first half-period’s solution at <math>y(0)=\pm Y_0</math> is  [[File:Fig 2 Relaxation oscillations F = 4.png|thumb|right|middle|300px|Relaxation oscillations {{math|1=''F'' = 4}}]]

<math display=block>\begin{align}
y(t) &= \begin{cases} 
y_1(t), & 0\le t<T_0; \\[4pt] 
y_2(t), & \displaystyle T_0\le t< \frac{T}{2}. \end{cases} \\[4pt] 
y_1(t) &= A_{1,k}\cdot \exp (s_{1,k}t)+A_{2,k}\cdot \exp (s_{2,k}t), \\[2pt]
y_2(t) &= A_{3,k}\cdot \exp(s_{3,k}t)+A_{4,k}\cdot \exp (s_{4,k}t).
\end{align}</math>

The second half-period’s solution is

<math display=block> y(t)= \begin{cases} 
\displaystyle -y_1\left(t-\frac{T}{2}\right), & \displaystyle \frac{T}{2} \le t < \frac{T}{2} + T_0; \\[4pt] 
\displaystyle -y_2\left(t-\frac{T}{2}\right), & \displaystyle \frac{T}{2} +  T_0 \le t < T. \end{cases} </math>

The solution contains four [[Constant of integration|constants of integration]] {{math|''A''{{sub|1}}, ''A''{{sub|2}}, ''A''{{sub|3}}, ''A''{{sub|4}}}}, the period {{mvar|T}} and the boundary {{math|''T''{{sub|0}}}} between {{math|''y''{{sub|1}}(''t'')}} and {{math|''y''{{sub|2}}(''t'')}} needs to be found. A boundary condition is derived from the continuity of {{math|''y''(''t'')}} and {{math|''dy''/''dt''}}.<ref>Pilipenko A. M., and Biryukov V. N. «Investigation of Modern Numerical Analysis Methods of Self-Oscillatory Circuits Efficiency», Journal of Radio Electronics, No 9, (2013). http://jre.cplire.ru/jre/aug13/9/text-engl.html</ref>

Solution of (1) in the stationary mode thus is obtained by solving a system of algebraic equations as

<math display=block>\begin{array}{ll}
& y_1(0) = -Y_0 & y_1(T_0) = Y_0 \\[6pt]
& y_2(T_0) = Y_0 & y_2 \! \left(\tfrac{T}{2}\right) = Y_0 \\[6pt]
& \displaystyle \left.\frac{dy_1}{dt}\right|_{T_0} = \left.\frac{dy_2}{dt}\right|_{T_0} \qquad 
& \displaystyle \left.\frac{dy_1}{dt}\right|_{0} = -\left.\frac{dy_2}{dt}\right|_\frac{T}{2}
\end{array}</math>

The integration constants are obtained by the [[Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm]]. 
With <math>f(y)=\mu(-1+y^2)</math>, <math>\mu = \text{const.} > 0,</math>  Eq. (1) named [[Van der Pol oscillator]]. Its solution cannot be expressed by [[Elementary function|elementary functions]] in closed form.
